# Parameter Walkthrough — What Each Estimate Is Doing (with the time terms put back in)

*Exploratory companion to the manuscript Tables 2 & 3. Generated by
`scripts/parameter_walkthrough_models.py`; raw numbers in
`data/generated/parameter_walkthrough.json`.*

## Why this document exists

The manuscript tables (`paper_table_models.py`) were pared down per PI direction
(2026-07): the cubic time polynomial (`time2`, `time3`) was dropped in favor of a
linear trend, and the two spending×time interactions (`SPEND_APP_z:time`,
`SPEND_WORK_z:time`) were removed. Only one interaction survived
(`pct_flc_z:time`, in the violations M3 column).

This walkthrough does the opposite: it **rebuilds both tables one variable at a
time and puts every dropped time term back in**, so we can watch — coefficient by
coefficient, variance component by variance component — exactly what each
parameter is doing, and in particular what the *time interactions* are doing to
everything else. It is a diagnostic / teaching artifact, **not** a new manuscript
specification. Nothing here changes the paper.

Two modelling choices (confirmed before building):

1. **All dropped time terms reintroduced** — cubic time (`time2`, `time3`) *and*
   the covariate×time interactions (`SPEND_APP_z:time`, `SPEND_WORK_z:time`,
   `pct_flc_z:time`), on **both** tables (the paper only ever put `pct_flc_z:time`
   on violations; here inspections gets the interaction row too, so the two tables
   are directly comparable).
2. **Fixed common sample.** Every step of a given table is fit on the *same*
   listwise-complete cases — the fullest model's sample (violations N = 320 obs /
   39 states; inspections N = 351 / 39). N never changes as covariates enter, so a
   change in a variance component is caused by the *specification*, not by states
   dropping in and out. (This differs from the paper, where each column uses its
   own N.)

Everything else follows project convention:
`MixedLM.from_formula(..., re_formula='~time').fit(method='lbfgs')` — REML, random
intercept **and** random slope on linear time by state.

---

## 1. The model skeleton — what the machine is estimating

For state *i* in year *t* the model is

```
DV_it = (β0 + u0_i)                      ← intercept  + state random intercept
      + (β_time + u1_i)·time_it          ← linear time slope + state random slope
      + β_time2·time²  + β_time3·time³   ← fixed curvature (spike shape)
      + Σ β_k · X_ki                     ← Level-2 covariate main effects (z-scored)
      + Σ β_j · (X_ji · time_it)         ← covariate×time cross-level interactions
      + e_it                             ← within-state residual
```

with the random parts distributed

```
[u0_i, u1_i] ~ N(0, G),   G = | σ²_u0    σ_u01 |     e_it ~ N(0, σ²_e)
                              | σ_u01   σ²_u1  |
```

So there are **four variance quantities**, and every fitted model reports all four:

| Symbol | statsmodels source | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **σ²_u0** | `cov_re.iloc[0,0]` | between-state variance in the *intercept* (level in 2017). This is the quantity the paper's pseudo-R² acts on. |
| **σ²_u1** | `cov_re.iloc[1,1]` | between-state variance in the *time slope* — how much states differ in their year-over-year trajectory. |
| **σ_u01** | `cov_re.iloc[0,1]` | covariance of a state's level and its slope. |
| **σ²_e** | `res.scale` | within-state (residual) variance — year-to-year noise around a state's own line. |
| ICC₀ | derived | σ²_u0 / (σ²_u0 + σ²_e) — share of variance that is between-state *at time 0* (2017). |

**The single most important thing to internalize: time is centered at 2017**
(`time = year − 2017`, so 2011 → −6, 2017 → 0, 2019 → +2). Centering is what makes
every other coefficient readable, and it is the entire reason the interactions
change the other estimates:

- **Intercept** = predicted DV in **2017**, for an average state (all z-covariates
  = 0; for violations also inspections = 0 — an extrapolation, see §3).
- **A covariate main effect β_k is the effect of that covariate in 2017 only** —
  the value of the slope of DV-on-X at `time = 0`. It is *not* a time-averaged
  effect once an ×time term is present.
- **A covariate×time coefficient β_j is the per-year change in that covariate's
  effect.** The full marginal effect of covariate X in a given year is
  `β_X + β_{X:time} · time`. In 2017 (`time = 0`) it collapses back to `β_X`.

That last block is the crux of "what is each parameter doing when the time
interactions are in there," and §5 is devoted to it.

> **AIC/BIC note.** These are REML fits, so AIC/BIC are `nan` / not comparable
> across specifications with different fixed effects (same caveat as
> `docs/transform_exploration.md`). We judge fit by the *variance components* and
> pseudo-R² on σ²_u0, not by information criteria.

---

## 2. Reading a step

Each step **adds one variable (or one tightly-coupled pair) to the running
model** and reports the new term's estimate plus all four variance components.
`pseudo-R²` is `(σ²_u0_baseline − σ²_u0_step) / σ²_u0_baseline`, i.e. the paper's
between-state-intercept-variance-reduction metric, computed against a fixed
baseline fit on the same common sample:

- **Inspections baseline** = `inspections ~ time` (linear time only).
- **Violations baseline** = `violations ~ inspections + time` (the paper's
  matched-N convention: inspections + linear time).

Because the violations baseline *already contains inspections and linear time*,
the earliest violations steps (which don't yet contain those) can show a
**negative** pseudo-R². That is expected — it is telling us those Level-1 controls
themselves carry between-state variance (more in §3).

---

## 3. TABLE 3 — Violations, variable by variable

Baseline σ²_u0 (`inspections + time`) = **211.75**. Common sample N = 320 (39 states).

| Step | Added | Added term b (p) | σ²_u0 | σ²_u1 | pseudo-R² |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | `time` | +1.92 (<.001)*** | 245.87 | 4.69 | −16.1% |
| 1 | `time2`, `time3` | −1.12***, −0.21*** | 208.71 | 3.81 | +1.4% |
| 2 | `inspections` | +0.133 (<.001)*** | 225.66 | 5.21 | −6.6% |
| 3 | `SPEND_APP_z` | −1.97 (.256) | 180.23 | 4.15 | +14.9% |
| 4 | `SPEND_WORK_z` | −2.23 (.096)+ | 161.98 | 3.97 | +23.5% |
| 5 | `lii_2017_z` | −0.06 (.975) | 162.87 | 3.92 | +23.1% |
| 6 | `h2a_per_farmworker_z` | −0.22 (.860) | 168.56 | 3.99 | +20.4% |
| 7 | `dol_demand_met_pct_z` | +0.09 (.950) | 160.59 | 3.75 | +24.2% |
| 8 | `pct_flc_z` | +2.28 (.222) | 162.33 | 3.12 | +23.3% |
| 9 | `SPEND_APP_z:time` | **−1.05 (.020)*** | 159.71 | 3.20 | +24.6% |
| 10 | `SPEND_WORK_z:time` | −0.52 (.239) | 158.83 | 3.52 | +25.0% |
| 11 | `pct_flc_z:time` | +0.43 (.314) | 158.96 | 3.61 | +24.9% |

**Step 0 — `time` (linear).** +1.92*** says that, ignoring curvature, violations
rise ~1.9 per state per year on average. But σ²_u0 = 245.87 is *above* the
baseline (211.75), hence −16.1%: a straight line is a poor description of the
2016–17 spike, and the misfit is dumped into the between-state intercept term.

**Step 1 — `time2`, `time3` (the reintroduced cubic).** Both are strongly
significant (−1.12***, −0.21***) — this is the real news of the whole exercise.
The **negative quadratic** makes the trajectory *concave* (a hump that rises then
falls — the 2016–17 peak), and the **negative cubic** makes it *asymmetric* (the
climb and the descent have different steepness). Adding them drops σ²_u0 from
245.87 → 208.71 (now +1.4% vs baseline) and σ²_e from 138.84 → 133.81: the curve
that used to be misattributed to "some states are just higher" is now correctly
attributed to *time*. **This is direct evidence that the manuscript's linear-time
simplification throws away real, highly significant structure** — a fact worth
stating plainly even though the paper keeps linear time by PI direction.

**Step 2 — `inspections`.** +0.133*** — each additional inspection in a state-year
is associated with ~0.13 more violations (an enforcement-exposure control: more
looking finds more). Note σ²_u0 goes *up* (208.71 → 225.66, pseudo-R² −6.6%).
Adding a **Level-1 (time-varying)** predictor is not guaranteed to lower the
**Level-2** intercept variance; here it slightly inflates it. This is the same
non-monotone behavior documented in `docs/variance_decomposition.md` and is why
the paper's violations baseline *includes* inspections — so its Δσ² is measured
from an inspections-adjusted starting point, not credited to inspections.

**Steps 3–4 — the spending block does the real work.** `SPEND_APP_z` alone drops
σ²_u0 to 180.23 (+14.9%); adding `SPEND_WORK_z` drops it to 161.98 (+23.5%). These
two FIFRA-protected-population spending denominators are the workhorse
between-state predictors, exactly as the manuscript claims. Note the main-effect
estimates here (−1.97 ns, −2.23+) are *time-averaged* effects — no interaction is
in the model yet, so β is a single pooled slope across all years.

**Steps 5–8 — LII, H-2A block.** `lii_2017_z`, `h2a_per_farmworker_z`,
`dol_demand_met_pct_z` each move σ²_u0 by well under a percentage point and are all
non-significant: on this sample they add essentially nothing between states once
spending is in. `pct_flc_z` (+2.28, ns *as a main effect*) is the interesting one —
hold that thought for step 11.

**Steps 9–11 — the reintroduced time interactions.** Watch two things:

- **`SPEND_APP_z:time` = −1.05, p = .020 — significant.** And it *re-writes its own
  main effect*: at step 3 `SPEND_APP_z` was −1.97 (ns); the moment the interaction
  enters (step 9) the main effect jumps to **−5.03 (p = .066)**. Nothing about the
  data changed — the main effect was simply *re-centered onto 2017*. Reading them
  together: in 2017 a 1-SD-higher spending-per-applicator state sits ~5 violations
  lower, and that gap **widens by ~1 more violation for every year past 2017**
  (and correspondingly was smaller before 2017). So the spending "effect" is not
  flat — it grows across the study window. This is precisely the substantive story
  the interaction is there to tell.
- **σ²_u1 barely moves** (3.12 → 3.20 → 3.52 → 3.61). For violations the
  cross-level interactions do *not* soak up much between-state *slope* variance —
  contrast this with inspections in §4, where they do.

**Final full violations model** (all terms, common sample):

| term | b | se | p | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Intercept | +14.19 | 2.64 | <.0001 | *** |
| time | +2.54 | 0.60 | <.0001 | *** |
| time2 | −1.11 | 0.32 | .0006 | *** |
| time3 | −0.21 | 0.05 | <.0001 | *** |
| inspections | +0.124 | 0.040 | .0020 | ** |
| SPEND_APP_z | −3.01 | 2.99 | .314 | |
| SPEND_WORK_z | −4.73 | 2.56 | .064 | + |
| lii_2017_z | −0.14 | 1.93 | .942 | |
| h2a_per_farmworker_z | −0.23 | 1.33 | .860 | |
| dol_demand_met_pct_z | +1.64 | 1.68 | .328 | |
| pct_flc_z | +4.49 | 2.49 | .071 | + |
| SPEND_APP_z:time | −0.64 | 0.54 | .239 | |
| SPEND_WORK_z:time | −0.57 | 0.44 | .199 | |
| pct_flc_z:time | +0.43 | 0.43 | .314 | |

Note the collinearity lesson: `SPEND_APP_z:time` was significant *alone* (step 9,
−1.05*) but is *not* significant in the full model (−0.64, .239). The three ×time
terms compete for the same "how do state gaps change over time" signal; entered
together, none is individually significant even though the first one was on its
own. This is a second reason the manuscript keeps only one interaction. (Intercept
caveat: 14.19 is the predicted 2017 count for an average state with **zero**
inspections — an out-of-range extrapolation, since no state has zero inspections;
read it as a regression anchor, not a real prediction.)

## 4. TABLE 2 — Inspections, variable by variable

Baseline σ²_u0 (`time`) = **810.84**. Common sample N = 351 (39 states).

| Step | Added | Added term b (p) | σ²_u0 | σ²_u1 | pseudo-R² |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | `time` | −0.71 (.300) | 810.84 | 15.97 | +0.0% |
| 1 | `time2`, `time3` | −0.30 (.352), −0.02 (.729) | 810.97 | 15.98 | −0.0% |
| 2 | `SPEND_APP_z` | −9.99 (.013)* | 806.05 | 23.45 | +0.6% |
| 3 | `SPEND_WORK_z` | −2.59 (.496) | 807.92 | 23.95 | +0.4% |
| 4 | `lii_2017_z` | −4.68 (.372) | 810.14 | 23.99 | +0.1% |
| 5 | `h2a_per_farmworker_z` | +4.48 (.214) | 810.85 | 23.56 | −0.0% |
| 6 | `dol_demand_met_pct_z` | +0.88 (.838) | 814.25 | 23.29 | −0.4% |
| 7 | `pct_flc_z` | −2.53 (.570) | 817.87 | 22.46 | −0.9% |
| 8 | `SPEND_APP_z:time` | +0.29 (.729) | 847.03 | **17.49** | −4.5% |
| 9 | `SPEND_WORK_z:time` | +0.04 (.966) | 872.08 | 18.27 | −7.6% |
| 10 | `pct_flc_z:time` | +0.83 (.280) | 869.72 | **16.84** | −7.3% |

The inspections story is almost the mirror image, and it is exactly why the PI
dropped these terms for this outcome:

**Cubic time is inert here.** `time2` (−0.30, .352) and `time3` (−0.02, .729) are
both non-significant — inspections have no 2016–17 spike to fit, so the polynomial
that was essential for violations does nothing here. σ²_u0 doesn't budge. (This
independently confirms that keeping inspections linear, per PI direction, costs
nothing.)

**Level-2 covariates explain ~zero between-state variance.** ICC₀ sits at ~0.85–0.86
throughout — the between-state share of variance is enormous and *immovable*. The
best any covariate manages is `SPEND_APP_z` at +0.6% (and it's significant on its
own, −9.99*), after which every addition wobbles around zero and several go
**negative**. In a mixed model σ²_u0 is a re-estimated parameter, not a residual
sum of squares, so it is not bounded to fall when predictors are added; a small
negative pseudo-R² means the predictor explains *nothing* between states and the
re-fit nudges the variance slightly upward. This is the "negative Δσ²" the
manuscript reports as-is for inspections.

**The interactions actively hurt — but they reveal what σ²_u1 is for.** Adding the
three ×time terms drives σ²_u0 *up* by 7% (pseudo-R² −4.5% → −7.6% → −7.3%) with
every interaction coefficient non-significant: pure instability, no signal. **But
look at σ²_u1:** it drops from 22.46 (step 7) to 17.49 (step 8) to 16.84 (step 10).
That is the mechanism worth understanding — see §5.3. The fixed ×time coefficients
are absorbing part of the *random slope* variance (states differing in their
inspection trajectory), even while they inflate the *intercept* variance and
explain nothing useful. For inspections this is a bad trade, which is why the terms
were cut.

**Final full inspections model:** Intercept +28.15***, time −1.63+, everything else
non-significant (`SPEND_APP_z` −6.97, `SPEND_WORK_z` −5.82, `lii_2017_z` −4.15,
`h2a_per_farmworker_z` +4.89, `dol_demand_met_pct_z` −1.17, `pct_flc_z` +0.56,
`SPEND_APP_z:time` +0.68, `SPEND_WORK_z:time` −0.06, `pct_flc_z:time` +0.83).
Note `SPEND_APP_z` was −9.99* alone (step 2) but −6.97 ns in the full model — same
collinearity-driven attenuation seen in violations.

---

## 5. Deep dive — what the TIME INTERACTIONS specifically do

This section collects the three distinct jobs an ×time interaction performs, each
demonstrated by a number from the runs above.

### 5.1 They re-center every main effect onto 2017

Without an interaction, `β_X` is a **single pooled slope** — one number summarizing
X's association with the DV averaged across all nine years. Add `X:time` and `β_X`
becomes the **2017 slice** (the effect at `time = 0`), while `β_{X:time}` carries
"how much that effect changes per year." The total effect of X in any year is:

```
effect_of_X(year) = β_X + β_{X:time} · (year − 2017)
```

Cleanest demonstration — `SPEND_APP_z` in violations:

| model state | `SPEND_APP_z` (main) | `SPEND_APP_z:time` |
|---|---:|---:|
| step 3 (no interaction) | −1.97 (ns) — *pooled/time-averaged* | — |
| step 9 (interaction in) | **−5.03 (.066)** — *2017-specific* | −1.05 (.020)* |

The main effect more than doubled and gained significance the instant the
interaction appeared. The data are identical; only the *meaning* of `β_X` changed.
Reading step 9: in 2017, a 1-SD-higher-spending state has ~5 fewer violations; the
gap grows ~1 further per year afterward (e.g. by 2019, ≈ −5.03 + (−1.05)(2) ≈ −7.1;
back in 2011, ≈ −5.03 + (−1.05)(−6) ≈ +1.3). **A single "spending effect" number
would have hidden this trajectory entirely.**

Same phenomenon for `pct_flc_z` in violations: as a bare main effect it is +2.28
(ns, step 8); alongside `pct_flc_z:time` in the manuscript's linear M3 it is
+5.29*. The FLC-composition association is concentrated around the 2017 spike, so
its 2017-centered value is much larger than its all-years average.

### 5.2 An interaction's own significance is context-dependent (collinearity)

`SPEND_APP_z:time` is −1.05* (p = .020) when it is the *only* interaction present
(step 9) but −0.64 (p = .239) in the full model (steps 10–11 add two more ×time
terms). The three interactions all encode "how do between-state gaps evolve over
time," and they are collinear; entered together they split the credit and none
survives individually. **Conclusion: you cannot read the significance of one ×time
term without knowing which other ×time terms share the model.** This is the
statistical justification for the manuscript keeping exactly one interaction rather
than the full set.

### 5.3 Interactions explain *slope* variance (σ²_u1), not intercept variance (σ²_u0)

A covariate main effect is a Level-2 predictor of the **random intercept** — it
competes with `u0_i`, so it shows up in σ²_u0 (and hence in pseudo-R²). A
covariate×time interaction is a Level-2 predictor of the **random slope** — it
competes with `u1_i`, so its payoff appears in **σ²_u1**, which pseudo-R² never
looks at. Inspections shows this crisply: the three ×time terms cut σ²_u1 from
22.46 → 16.84 (a ~25% reduction in slope heterogeneity) while *raising* σ²_u0.

**This is a blind spot in the paper's headline metric.** Pseudo-R² is defined on
σ²_u0 only, so it structurally *cannot reward* an interaction that does its job on
the slope. An ×time term can be genuinely explanatory (reduce σ²_u1) yet post a
zero or negative pseudo-R². When judging interactions, look at σ²_u1, not the
pseudo-R² column. (For violations the σ²_u1 reduction is small, so here the
interactions are weak on *both* fronts — consistent with dropping all but one.)

### 5.4 The cubic time terms are not interactions, but they are the biggest "time" finding

`time2`/`time3` are fixed **curvature**, not cross-level interactions, but they are
the most consequential reintroduced terms: both are p < .001 for violations
(concave, asymmetric peak) and both are non-significant for inspections. The
asymmetric 2016–17 violation spike is *real, large, and highly significant
structure* that the manuscript's linear specification (by PI direction) does not
capture. That is a defensible editorial choice — a linear trend is simpler and the
paper's spending story lives in the between-state variance, not the time shape —
but this walkthrough documents precisely what is being left on the table.

---

## 6. Reconciling with the manuscript (why the paper is still right to drop them)

Nothing here contradicts the PI's decisions; it explains their cost and benefit:

| Term | What it does (this walkthrough) | Why the paper drops/keeps it |
|---|---|---|
| `time2`, `time3` (violations) | Highly significant; captures the real asymmetric spike; lowers σ²_u0 and σ²_e | Dropped for a simpler, communicable linear trend; the spending finding does not depend on the time shape |
| `time2`, `time3` (inspections) | Non-significant; inert | Correctly dropped — no spike to fit |
| `SPEND_APP_z:time` | Significant alone, re-centers spending onto 2017, but collinear with the other ×time terms and dies in the full model | Dropped — not robust once the interaction set competes |
| `SPEND_WORK_z:time` | Never significant | Dropped |
| `pct_flc_z:time` | Non-significant here (cubic model) but the surviving term in the paper's linear M3 | Kept as the single, theory-motivated interaction |
| ×time terms (inspections) | Inflate σ²_u0, only touch σ²_u1, all non-significant | Correctly dropped — pure instability for this outcome |

**One caveat the walkthrough surfaces that the paper's metric hides:** pseudo-R²
lives on σ²_u0, so it under-credits any interaction whose real effect is on the
slope variance σ²_u1 (§5.3). If a reviewer asks whether the interactions were
fairly evaluated, the honest answer is that the σ²_u1 evidence should be shown too
— and it still supports dropping them for inspections and keeping only one for
violations.

---

## 7. Reproduce

```bash
# needs data/generated/spend_bls_variables.csv (run spending_bls_models.py first)
python3 scripts/parameter_walkthrough_models.py
# → prints both build-ups; writes data/generated/parameter_walkthrough.json
```

Full per-step coefficient blocks (every term, not just the newly-added one) are in
`data/generated/parameter_walkthrough.json` under `inspections.steps[*].params`
and `violations.steps[*].params`.
